Day 25 of 100 · Infrastructure Automation

First Ansible Playbook

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityInfrastructure AutomationTopic verified by artifact

The first playbook moved from one-off commands to a declarative file that maps hosts to tasks and desired state.

Architecture / mental model

Playbook → play → target hosts → ordered tasks → module results

How it works

A play binds a host pattern to a list of tasks. Each task calls a module with parameters that describe the state or action required.

Using modules such as package, file, copy and service is preferable to hiding everything behind shell commands because modules can report whether they actually changed state.

A playbook also becomes documentation: another engineer can see what the machine is supposed to look like instead of reverse-engineering it from the machine itself.

Hands-on reference

ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml
ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml --check

Verification

Run the playbook once, inspect changed/ok results, then run it again. A well-designed state-oriented play should converge and show fewer or no changes on the second run.

Field note / gotcha

Check mode is useful, not omniscient. Some modules cannot fully predict changes and external side effects may not be represented.

Security considerations

Review `become` usage and task scope. A playbook can reproduce a privilege mistake across an entire fleet with impressive consistency.

What I learned

Repeatability is the first visible benefit of infrastructure as code; idempotence is what makes repeatability safe.
